To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
skin conductance response (SCR) is not an accurate tool to measure pain during CTR, but it is a reliable tool to measure anxiety during CTR.
skin conductance responses (SCR) per second during a standardized painful procedure (CTR) were not significantly different between pain (P‐SCR) and anxiety (ASCR) states.
SCR during CTR correlated with A‐VAS and P‐VAS, but not with heart rate or respiratory rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions:   1.
the development of a new method of pain measurement based on the electrical conductivity of the skin, which is known as skin conductance response.
the development of a novel, noninvasive, non-contact, and low cost skin conductance measurement method based on a single frequency microwave system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SCR during CTR is not a valid tool for assessing pain or anxiety.
there is insufficient evidence to support the use of SCR during CTR.
there is a significant positive correlation between the SCR and P‐VAS and A‐VAS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SCR is a promising tool to assess pain and anxiety during CTR.
the skin conductance response per second is not an accurate measure of pain during chest tube removal.
the skin conductance response per second (SCRs) is not a reliable pain assessment tool during CTR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SCR is not a good measure of pain during CTR.
the SCR is an objective measure of anxiety and pain, and can be used as an adjunct to the VAS to assess these two variables.
skin conductance variability is not a valid tool for assessing pain in adults undergoing CTR.
